record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analysis to robotics models and downstream task success rates, using a different setting and performance measure from language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports aggregate fitted exponents, confidence intervals, and fit statistics for data, model-size, and compute scaling. Its main measure is downstream error rate (100 − success rate), not held-out cross-entropy. It says it does not aim to estimate scaling laws for predicting performance from specific inputs. The emergent-capability counts are included separately as findings not covered by the versions.
record.test_reason: This is a meta-analysis of 327 robotics papers. It fits a power law, with an offset, to each scaling ablation of downstream task error (100 − success rate) against data, model size or compute, then aggregates the exponents. It is a new setting (robot foundation models, and LLMs used for robotics) with results on downstream predictability (V6) and on how exponents depend on setup and fitting choices (V7). No held-out pretraining loss is measured, so V1–V5 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right. The authors conclude that power laws describe how robotics task error falls with data, model size and compute, with diminishing returns, and that exponents vary by task and architecture. They find pretraining more compute-efficient than fine-tuning and note that robotics exponents exceed those of language models, comparable to vision. They report emergent capabilities, and flag sparse, non-standardised studies with few data points as the main limitation.
record.recipe_differences: Meta-analysis of robotics downstream success rates and fitted error-rate power laws, rather than controlled language-model pretraining runs measured by held-out cross-entropy. It does not test compute-optimal allocation or large-run extrapolation.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported exponents vary by model category, seen versus unseen tasks, simulated versus real robot settings, benchmark grouping, task, compute-scaling method, pretraining versus fine-tuning, and whether low-R2 fits are filtered out.

fits_no_version.finding: Emergent-capability cases (0% success at the smallest ablation, then success at larger scale): 10 of 125 model-size studies and 18 of 275 data studies. The authors say these were inconsistently replicated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some robotic capabilities appear only beyond a scale threshold in data or model-size ablations; such cases are a minority and not consistently replicated.

record.problems: The authors report that many scaling studies have only two or three data points, limiting coefficient estimation. Compute scaling comes from one source study. Tasks and success-rate definitions vary; some validation sets overlap training data. The analysis uses downstream success/error rather than held-out language-model loss and does not test out-of-sample prediction. Several categories have very small sample sizes.
record.rows_left_out: The appendix provides individual scaling-fit entries for many cited papers in Tables IX–XI. These per-study entries are not separately recorded here because the 60-row budget is prioritized for aggregate estimates, condition-dependent results, fit comparisons, and emergent-capability counts.

untested.parts: All of it: no held-out pretraining loss is measured.
All of it: no out-of-sample extrapolation; the authors say they do not aim to predict performance.
All of it: no compute-optimal allocation.
All of it: no shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
A loss-type power law in other modalities or regimes. Only downstream robot success error is measured.
Downstream performance against pretraining loss; actual predictive accuracy on held-out larger scales; behaviour over several orders of magnitude within one study (the median study spans about 10x).
Language-model exponents under different parameter-counting or schedule choices; the compute-optimal split; bending of curves within a study.

missing.what: Subgroups whose CIs cross zero, contrary to scaling: model-size PVR, Seen, Unseen and Simulated Robot; compute Spatial Tasks and Object Tasks
Data-scaling rows by deployment: Simulated −0.262, Real Robot −0.357, Benchmark −0.250; model-size Real Robot −0.300 and Benchmark −0.215
Selection rule: only fits with −1<α,β,γ<0 (87% of studies) are analysed, so non-improving fits are excluded from the aggregates
R² filter effect on model-size VLA (−0.238 to −0.368) and on the compute fine-tuning subgroup (−0.109 to −0.126)
Range of the scaling studies: median max/min ratio of about 10x for data and model size and 50x for compute; overall compute span 2.4 orders of magnitude

record.verdict_notes: I linked the rows to V6 (downstream improvement with scale) and V7 (setup and fit dependence), and removed V5 because no loss-type measure is used. One could argue that robotics fine-tuning counts toward V5. Key caveats: most fits have 3 points and 3 parameters; ranges are narrow (about 10x); there is no held-out prediction; the −1<α<0 selection biases the aggregates toward improvement; compute rests on a single source paper. R13 and R15 appear to duplicate each other.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small runs predict losses of much larger runs; the paper states it does not aim to estimate performance from specific inputs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and how its split changes with compute.
Controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests downstream robotic task success/error scaling in RFMs and LLMs used in robotics, not the same law for image/video models, repeated data, or other non-robotics modalities and regimes.
Tests downstream task success/error against scale, not downstream performance against pretraining loss or out-of-sample prediction accuracy.

Reports setup-dependent exponents and fitting limitations in robotics; does not test published language-model exponents under alternative parameter-counting or fitting choices, nor whether curves bend away from a single power law.
